answer: That release replaced the hover-icon plot viewer with click-to-expand: click (single- or double-click depending on build) the inline PNG output to open it full-size, no separate icon needed anymore. Make sure the figure is actually rendered as a static PNG (`%matplotlib inline`), not through an interactive backend like `%matplotlib widget`, since widget output isn't a clickable image. If clicking still does nothing, this was a known regression in the Jupyter extension around that date -- update the Python and Jupyter extensions to the latest version (it was fixed in a follow-up release). As a workaround, right-click the output and use 'Save Image As' to view it externally at full resolution, and check that 'jupyter.enablePlotViewer' isn't disabled in settings.

Setting `number_format='@'` only changes display formatting; Excel's green-triangle 'number stored as text' warning is a separate heuristic applied whenever a text cell's content parses as a number, independent of the format code, so it persists regardless. There's no pure formatting fix. Two real options: (1) write the value as a formula that evaluates to text, e.g. `cell.value = '="00123"'` -- Excel then treats it as a formula result and suppresses the warning; or (2) have recipients disable the check: File > Options > Formulas > Error Checking Rules > uncheck 'Numbers formatted as text or preceded by an apostrophe'. Since the warning has zero functional effect and you control the writer but not every recipient's Excel settings, the formula-string trick is the most reliable way to suppress it directly in the file.

Don't loop in Python -- build a scipy sparse matrix from your dataframe and call sklearn's `cosine_similarity` once on the whole matrix; it uses sparse matrix multiplication and is far faster than manual O(N^2) pairwise calls:
```
from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
X = csr_matrix(df.drop(columns='p_Id').values)
sim = cosine_similarity(X, dense_output=False)  # sparse result
```
The 'scores display as 0' issue is almost certainly a display/rounding artifact, not an actual zero -- pandas/numpy truncate printed decimals by default. Check the raw float, not the printed one: `np.set_printoptions(precision=10)` or `pd.set_option('display.float_format', '{:.8f}'.format)`. The output is still O(N^2) in size, but computed as one vectorized call instead of nested Python loops, which was the actual bottleneck.

`gr.Progress()` drives Gradio's single global progress overlay tied to the queue, not to any particular tab's component -- that's why it shows on every tab. For a per-tab bar, don't rely on the built-in tracker; add a dedicated `gr.Textbox`/`gr.HTML` inside each tab as an explicit output, and update it manually from a generator function:
```
def generate(prompt):
    for i in range(steps):
        ...
        yield gr.update(value=f'{i}/{steps}'), None
    yield gr.update(value='done'), final_image
btn.click(generate, inputs=[...], outputs=[tab_progress_box, tab_image])
```
Because `outputs` is scoped to that tab's own components, only that tab's textbox updates no matter what other tabs are doing concurrently. Repeat per tab with its own progress/output pair.

`errors='ignore'` only silences the error at the whole-Series level -- if even one element fails to match your `format`, pandas aborts the whole conversion and returns the original Series unchanged; it does not fall back per-element. That's why 'ignore' looks like a no-op while 'coerce' converts successfully but turns every non-match into NaT. To keep original text where it isn't a date and get real datetimes where it is:
```
parsed = pd.to_datetime(result['Action'], format='%A %B %d %Y', errors='coerce')
result['Action'] = parsed.fillna(result['Action'])
```
This yields an object column mixing Timestamp and original strings, which is what you want. Note `errors='ignore'` is deprecated/removed in recent pandas specifically because this behavior confuses people.

Both relationships use `lazy='select'`, so neither is eagerly joined at the SQL level -- the 'auto-loading' you see is a lazy load fired the instant something accesses the attribute. Likely cause: your Pydantic response model for User includes `items` (so `from_attributes`/`orm_mode` serialization touches `user.items`, triggering the lazy SELECT), but never references `datastreams` anywhere, so it's simply never accessed and never loaded -- nothing to do with the relationship definitions, which are identical. Check the schema(s) you actually return from the endpoint. To confirm, temporarily set `lazy='raise'` on both relationships -- accessing an unintended one throws instead of silently querying, making every access site easy to find. Use `selectinload`/`joinedload` explicitly in the query when you do want eager loading.

`list.append()` mutates the list in place and returns `None` -- that's why `codes` becomes `None` after `codes = codes.append(code)`. Drop the reassignment:
```
code = 'abc'
codes = []
if code != '':
    codes.append(code)
print(codes)  # ['abc']
```
If you just want a one-element list from a string directly, `codes = [code]` does the same thing without a loop.

Use the Level-5 rows' ID as the fill value and forward-fill it down through the following Level-8 rows:
```
df['Upper_ID'] = df['ID'].where(df['Level'] == 5).ffill()
```
`.where(df['Level']==5)` keeps `ID` only on rows where Level is 5 and sets everything else to NaN; `.ffill()` then propagates each Level-5 ID forward until the next Level-5 row overwrites it. Since your dataframe is already ordered so each Level-5 row precedes its Level-8 children, this correctly assigns 'A' down through the first block and 'B' through the next.

This isn't your code, it's a version-mismatch inside the `google-cloud-bigquery` install -- `schema.py` expects `google.cloud.bigquery_v2.types.StandardSqlDataType` to expose `.STRING` etc., but an incompatible/stale `google-cloud-bigquery-storage`, `proto-plus`, or `googleapis-common-protos` package installed alongside it changed that enum's shape, so the attribute is missing at import time. Fix by upgrading the whole BigQuery stack together, not just `google-cloud-bigquery`:
```
pip install --upgrade google-cloud-bigquery google-cloud-bigquery-storage pandas-gbq proto-plus googleapis-common-protos db-dtypes
```
If that doesn't clear it, uninstall all of them and reinstall fresh in a clean virtualenv/conda env -- old cached wheels across multiple environments (you're on an anaconda3 base env) commonly leave mismatched versions shadowing each other. Also confirm no local file/module in your project is named `types.py` or `google.py`, which would shadow the real package.

Two separate bugs. First, `line.strip('')` strips nothing -- an empty argument means 'no characters to strip', not whitespace; call `.strip()` with no arguments to remove the trailing newline. Second, your expected output nests each field as its own single-item list, not a flat list of strings, so wrap each split value:
```
listID = []
with open('/Users/file.txt') as f:
    for line in f:
        fields = line.strip().split('\t')
        listID.append([[x] for x in fields])
```
This gives, per line, `[['Barcode1'], ['ID644'], ['79']]` as in your expected output, with no leftover newline on the last field.

'Nested' only multiplies complexities when one loop's iteration count is itself driven by running a whole other loop inside it. Here, `if i in liste_b` (O(n)) and `liste_b.remove(i)` (O(n)) aren't nested inside each other -- they're two sequential O(n) operations that each run at most once per outer-loop pass. Per outer iteration: O(n) [membership test] + O(n) [remove] = O(2n) = O(n). That O(n) cost per iteration, times n outer iterations, gives O(n^2), not O(n^3). You'd only get O(n^3) if the remove itself triggered another full O(n) loop for every element examined by the membership test -- true nesting -- which isn't happening; these are two separate linear passes stacked in sequence inside one loop, and sequential costs add rather than multiply.

Compute row sums and column sums once, then combine them and subtract the cell's own value since it's counted in both:
```
import numpy as np
row_sum = df.sum(axis=1).values
col_sum = df.sum(axis=0).values
combined = pd.DataFrame(row_sum[:, None] + col_sum[None, :] - df.values,
                         index=df.index, columns=df.columns)
```
For your example, cell (0,'a')=1 gets row_sum=4 + col_sum=9 - 1 = 12. This is O(rows x cols), the same order as the DataFrame itself, since row/col sums are computed once and broadcast instead of recomputed per cell -- much better than iterating and summing for every cell individually.

This error means `get_object()` couldn't find a `pk` or `slug` kwarg with those exact names coming out of URL resolution -- either your `urls.py` path converter uses a different kwarg name (e.g. `<slug:location>` instead of `<slug:slug>`), or extra kwargs (like the date) are being passed without also passing `pk`/`slug`. The body doesn't show `urls.py` or the view's `get_object`/`get_queryset`, so I can't confirm which, but the fix is either renaming the URL kwarg to `slug` (or `pk`), or telling the view about your custom name explicitly:
```
class DailyForecastDetailView(DetailView):
    model = Location
    slug_field = 'slug'
    slug_url_kwarg = 'your_url_kwarg_name'
```
Set `slug_field`/`slug_url_kwarg` (or `pk_url_kwarg`) to match whatever name your URL pattern actually captures.

Grayskull doesn't stay fully offline even for a local sdist -- it still calls out for supplementary metadata, notably the GitHub API to resolve repo/license info from the project URL. On your laptop those calls are fast; in CI, the most common cause of a ~20-minute blowup is GitHub API rate-limiting -- unauthenticated requests from a shared CI runner IP get throttled hard and Grayskull retries/backs off repeatedly. Set a `GITHUB_TOKEN` env var (Grayskull picks it up for authenticated GitHub requests) before running; that raises your rate limit from 60/hr to 5000/hr and should collapse the runtime back to seconds. If it's still slow afterward, check CI proxy/DNS latency to pypi.org and github.com specifically -- Grayskull has no documented fully-offline flag, since network calls for metadata enrichment are baked into its normal flow.

There's no fairness guarantee in `threading.Lock` -- it's a thin wrapper over the OS mutex/semaphore, and which waiting thread gets woken on release is decided by the OS scheduler, not Python. On most platforms this favors whichever thread the kernel currently has 'hot' (cache-warm, recently run), so a thread that just released the lock and loops straight back to re-acquire it often wins again before the scheduler switches -- a classic starvation/'lock convoy' pattern, worse when one thread's critical section (`sleep(0.2)`) is longer, giving the scheduler more chances to reschedule that same thread while it holds or re-grabs the lock. Variables that matter: `sys.setswitchinterval()` (GIL release cadence), OS thread priority/niceness, CPU affinity, and how long each thread holds the lock. For actual fairness, don't rely on `Lock`; use explicit hand-off (e.g. two `Event`s or a bounded `Semaphore` pair) instead of contending on one shared lock.

There's no generic way to auto-infer field names for arbitrary CSV shapes -- JSON needs keys, and a bare CSV row only has positional values, so something has to define the schema per log type. Two practical options: (1) if each source stream has a fixed layout, hardcode a header list per pattern and pick it by a discriminator field, then `dict(zip(headers, row))`; (2) if the first line of each batch is an actual header row, use `csv.DictReader` directly:
```
import csv, io, json
def handler(record_text):
    reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(record_text), delimiter='|')
    return [json.dumps(row) for row in reader]
```
For the Firehose transform, base64-decode each record's payload, parse it with your per-pattern logic, then base64-encode the JSON result before returning it. Without a schema per pattern, arbitrary CSV-to-JSON is underspecified -- you need a mapping table keyed by log type.

The body cuts off before showing your actual `GridSearchCV` call, CV splitter, or the error itself, so a full diagnosis isn't possible from this alone, but the near-universal cause for 'custom estimator won't work with GridSearchCV' is that it doesn't satisfy sklearn's estimator contract: it needs `get_params`/`set_params` (inherit `sklearn.base.BaseEstimator`), and every constructor argument must be stored unmodified as `self.<name> = <name>` with no other logic in `__init__`. Your `EncoderGRU` only subclasses `nn.Module`, so `clone()`, which `GridSearchCV` calls internally, will fail. Fix: also inherit `BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin`, keep `__init__` purely param-storing, and implement `fit(self, X, y)`/`predict(self, X)`/`score`. Simpler: wrap the underlying `GRUNet` with `skorch.NeuralNetRegressor`, which already implements the full sklearn interface for PyTorch models and works directly with `GridSearchCV` and a custom `TimeSeriesSplit`.

`getItemClassiness` is defined as a method (its first parameter, `item`, is standing in for `self`, which you never declared), so calling it bare as `getItemClassiness(item)` looks up a global function of that name, which doesn't exist -- hence 'undefined name'. Fix both the definition and the call:
```
def getItemClassiness(self, item):
    if item == 'tophat':
        return 2
    ...
    return 0

def getClassiness(self):
    total = 0
    for item in self.items:
        total += self.getItemClassiness(item)
    return total
```
Methods inside a class must take `self` explicitly and be called as `self.method(...)` -- Python never implicitly makes sibling methods callable as bare names the way ordinary helper functions would be.

This is iterative DFS/backtracking using a plain list as a stack instead of recursion. Each entry `(current, left, right)` is a partial state: `left` = '(' still available to place, `right` = ')' still owed, equal to the number of currently-unmatched opens. Popping and pushing new states walks the same decision tree a recursive solution would (try adding '(' if any left, try adding ')' if any owed) -- it just uses the stack's LIFO order instead of the call stack, which is why it reads differently from a permutation-based approach. Whenever `right>0` it's always valid to close, because `right` only ever counts opens not yet closed, so validity is enforced structurally rather than checked afterward. When both counters hit 0 the string is complete and balanced, so it's appended to `result`. It only ever builds valid prefixes, avoiding the wasted invalid strings a permutation approach generates.
